#A coding agent on a machine

Claude or Codex working on a project on another machine, a VPS or a laptop, in ai-box, from the control page alone. No ssh: everything below is typed in the machine's Shell tab. The project here is space-worlds-game; put your own in its place.

What you have at the end:

  • ai-box set up and built on the machine
  • the project cloned there, with a key that may push to that repository and no other
  • a coding agent in it that goes on when the page is closed, the link drops or the ServiceMan agent restarts, and that you attach to again from any browser

#Before you start

  • A machine with the ServiceMan agent dialled in: Remotes, + Add remote and the command from its Install tab. Here it is called vps1.
  • Ubuntu, and a user on it with sudo: the agent's own user, which is the one the Shell opens as. ai-box runs as that user and needs no root after setup.
  • Write access to the repository on GitHub, to add a key to it.

Open vps1 on the control page, then its Shell tab. The Shell is a login shell in the agent user's home. It ends when the tab closes, so anything long (a build) goes into tmux, as in step 2.

#1. Set up ai-box

sudo apt install -y git tmux
git clone https://github.com/vbarbarosh/ai-box ~/ai-box
~/ai-box/bin/configure

bin/configure installs podman and what rootless podman needs, loads fuse and tun, and grants your user the subuids. Run it as yourself, not under sudo: it asks for your password once, and only when something is missing. Running it again changes nothing and says what is already there. ~/ai-box/bin/self-check lists what is still missing without changing anything.

#2. Build the image

The build takes a while, longer than a Shell tab is worth keeping open. Run it in tmux:

tmux new -s build '~/ai-box/bin/build; read -p "done, Enter to close"'

Close the tab if you like; open the Shell again later and tmux attach -t build. The image is called ai-box. Rebuild it often, since Claude and Codex change every few days:

cd ~/ai-box && git pull && bin/build

Its logins, history and image store are in ~/ai-box/data/, which a pull and a build leave alone.

#3. A key that may push

A deploy key: an ssh key that GitHub accepts for one repository only. One key per machine and repository, so taking one machine's access away is deleting one key on GitHub, and a key copied off that machine reaches nothing else.

On the machine:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C 'vps1 space-worlds-game' -f ~/.ssh/space-worlds-game
cat ~/.ssh/space-worlds-game.pub

-N '' leaves it without a passphrase: nobody is there to type one when the agent's work is pushed, and ai-box's push asks the machine's git with no terminal at all. The key is mode 600 in ~/.ssh, and no box sees it: ai-box mounts the project folder, never your home.

On GitHub, in the repository: Settings → Deploy keys → Add deploy key. Title vps1, the line cat printed as the key, tick Allow write access, Add key. Or from a computer where gh is logged in, with the .pub file copied there:

gh repo deploy-key add space-worlds-game.pub -R vbarbarosh/space-worlds-game --allow-write --title vps1

Back on the machine, give the key a host name of its own, so git uses it for this repository and your other keys for everything else:

cat >> ~/.ssh/config <<'EOF'

Host github.com-space-worlds-game
    HostName github.com
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/space-worlds-game
    IdentitiesOnly yes
EOF
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config
ssh -T github.com-space-worlds-game

The first ssh asks whether to trust github.com. Say yes only if the fingerprint it shows is on GitHub's list (ed25519: SHA256:+DiY3wvvV6TuJJhbpZisF/zLDA0zPMSvHdkr4UvCOqU). Then it answers:

Hi vbarbarosh/space-worlds-game! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

The repository's name in that line, not yours, is how a deploy key looks.

#4. Clone the project

mkdir -p ~/work
git clone github.com-space-worlds-game:vbarbarosh/space-worlds-game ~/work/space-worlds-game
cd ~/work/space-worlds-game
git config user.name 'Your Name'
git config user.email 'you@example.com'
git push --dry-run origin main

The address is the host name from step 3, so this clone pushes with that key. The dry run asks GitHub for write access and sends nothing: Everything up-to-date is the answer you want. ERROR: The key you are authenticating with has been marked as read only means Allow write access was not ticked.

Keep projects out of ~/repos: ai-box mounts that folder into every box it opens.

Install the project's own dependencies inside the box, where its toolchain is:

~/ai-box/bin/run bin/configure

#5. Log in, once per machine

cd ~/work/space-worlds-game
~/ai-box/bin/run claude

The first time, Claude asks you to log in: it prints an address, you open it on your laptop, and paste the code back into the Shell. For Codex, open the box with ~/ai-box/bin/run and type codex login --device-auth in it: it prints a code to type on the laptop. Both are the subscriptions' logins, no API key.

The logins are kept in ~/ai-box/data/ on this machine, so every box opened here is logged in from now on. Another machine logs in on its own; copying the files over is what ServiceMan's synced files are for, and they are not built yet (terminal services).

Leave Claude with /exit: the box closes with it. A box opened with a bare bin/run closes with exit.

#6. Start the agent so it stays

A coding agent in the Shell ends when the Shell does. Run it in tmux instead, and start tmux in a systemd scope of its own:

systemd-run --user --scope --unit=ai-space-worlds-game \
    tmux -L space-worlds-game new -d -s main -c ~/work/space-worlds-game
tmux -L space-worlds-game attach

and in the terminal that opens:

~/ai-box/bin/run claude
  • tmux keeps the terminal when nobody is attached: the agent goes on working with the tab closed, and an attach shows the whole screen as it is now, not the fragments of what was printed meanwhile.
  • The scope takes tmux out of the ServiceMan agent's own unit. Without it, tmux started from the Shell belongs to that unit, and stopping the unit would end the coding agent with it.
  • -L space-worlds-game gives the project a tmux server of its own, so it sits in its own scope however many other tmux sessions the machine has.

If systemd-run says Failed to connect to bus, the Shell has no XDG_RUNTIME_DIR: export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/$(id -u) and run it again.

Leave it running: Ctrl-b d detaches, or just close the tab. Later, from any browser, the Shell tab again and:

tmux -L space-worlds-game attach

When Claude exits, the shell in the project folder is still there; exit there ends the session, the tmux server and the scope. tmux -L space-worlds-game ls says whether it is running, and systemctl --user status ai-space-worlds-game.scope shows it with everything it runs, the box and the containers inside it included.

#7. Push

ai-box opens .git read-only, so the agent changes files and you make the commits, in a second tmux window (Ctrl-b c, and Ctrl-b n to go back) or a second Shell tab:

cd ~/work/space-worlds-game
git status
git add -p
git commit
git push

git push uses the deploy key from step 3.

ai-box is getting two commands for the agent itself: commit, which takes one patch and makes one commit of it, and push, which pushes the branch the box was started on and nothing else. A commit made that way is never rewritten. Both ask the machine's git outside the box, so they will push with this same key: nothing here changes when they arrive.

#Not here yet

  • The Visual Notes note of the project, at /notes in the box: it lives on your computer, and copying it to the machine and back is ServiceMan's part of terminal services, still a specification.
  • Sessions from the control page: a list of the coding agents on every machine, started and attached with a click, the box rebuilt on a clock. The same specification.
  • One login for every machine: synced files, the same specification.
